audits.title: Ctrl-Z: Controlling AI Agents via Resampling
audits.genuine_reason: Mostly a positive results summary of a control-protocol paper, but it reports that statistical ways of combining suspicion scores across steps barely beat the naive baseline and were fragile under red-teaming.
experiments: Cross-step aggregation of monitor scores (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, autoregressive surprise) for audit decisions
Attack policy that gives up after repeated deferral to the trusted model
audits.primary_experiment: Cross-step aggregation of monitor scores (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, autoregressive surprise) for audit decisions

hypothesis.evidence: Authors expected that combining past suspicion scores with statistical tests would easily beat judging only the current step's score.

claim_scope.evidence: Only the general BashBench monitoring setup is given; no data size, evaluation details or scale for these aggregation tests.

method.evidence: Names a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test and autoregressive surprise models for combining per-step scores, compared against using only the current step.

models.evidence: Untrusted model is GPT-4o mini, but the trusted monitor that produced the scores is described only as an 8-billion-parameter model, unnamed.

result_direction.evidence: Techniques gave only a marginal gain over the naive current-step baseline, far below the expected easy win.

failure_type.evidence: Authors suggest the monitor already folds earlier context into each score, so extra aggregation adds little; attackers could also exploit it.

quote.value: Ultimately, these techniques performed little better than just looking at the current step
quote.evidence: Contiguous fragment from the aggregation paragraph stating the negative result.

audits.notes: Summary of a larger paper; failed sub-experiments get one short passage each; a separate hackathon failed for operational reasons.

audits.title: J-Lens: A Failed Replication on GPT-2
audits.genuine_reason: The whole post reports the authors' own tests of J-Lens against Logit Lens on GPT-2, all with a negative outcome, plus several follow-up stress tests that did not rescue it.
experiments: J-Lens vs Logit Lens on GPT-2 small and medium
Token-frequency control for the rank metric
Sparsity thresholding of the fitted J
audits.primary_experiment: J-Lens vs Logit Lens on GPT-2 small and medium

hypothesis.evidence: Tested the J-Lens paper's claim that it fixes the Logit Lens's layer misalignment; authors expected it to win, especially on future-token prediction.

claim_scope.evidence: 30 sequences (150 in a refit), 60 held-out prompts, 11 small-model layers, 23 medium layers, two metrics; authors limit the claim to this scope.

method.evidence: Compares J-Lens against Logit Lens using median rank of the model's own next token and a future-token metric; checks included identity-matrix and gradient tests.

models.evidence: GPT-2 small (124M) and GPT-2 medium (355M in most places, 255M once); the post's own numbers conflict.

result_direction.evidence: Presented as a replication that did not hold: J-Lens scored worse than Logit Lens at every small-model layer and all but one medium layer.

failure_type.evidence: Authors conclude the lens fails on both GPT-2 sizes; implementation checks passed, and more data, tuning and scaling did not change the outcome.

quote.value: J-Lens does not work on GPT-2 small or medium
quote.evidence: Headline sentence of the result section.

audits.notes: Beginner author, AI-written code; GPT-2 medium size stated inconsistently; Logit Lens may be unusually strong on GPT-2.

audits.title: Negative Results on Group SAEs
audits.genuine_reason: The author says the project's results were mostly negative and unpublished, and the post is a write-up of what was tried and why none of it gave a compelling result.
experiments: Group SAEs on synthetic superposed circles
Group SAEs on GPT-2 layer 7 activations
Learned group space on synthetic co-occurrence data
audits.primary_experiment: Group SAEs on GPT-2 layer 7 activations

hypothesis.evidence: Hoped a modified sparsity penalty would let SAEs find multi-dimensional features directly, without clustering latents afterwards.

claim_scope.evidence: Names GPT-2 layer 7, a ReLU-SAE baseline and matched sparsity, but not dictionary width, group size, training data or token count for these runs.

method.evidence: Group SAEs with an L1-of-L2 group sparsity penalty over equal-sized groups, compared with ordinary ReLU SAEs; also checked months and weekdays circular subspaces.

models.evidence: GPT-2, layer 7 activations; the post does not give the GPT-2 size.

result_direction.evidence: Group SAEs gave slightly better variance and loss metrics and semantically related groups, but no interesting multi-dimensional structure beyond what clustering would likely find.

failure_type.evidence: The method broadly worked but yielded nothing useful beyond baselines; author lost interest after about three months and lists doubts about the approach.

quote.value: none of our results were that compelling
quote.evidence: Author's summary of the project's outcome, covering this experiment.

audits.notes: Written a year after the work; figures not in text; teammates' circuits and learned-group results excluded.

audits.title: [Summary] Progress Update #1 from the GDM Mech Interp Team
audits.genuine_reason: A short index of research snippets. The negative items (a ghost-grads replication, SAEs on Tracr and toy models, replicated dictionary-learning tweaks) get one to three sentences each, with no experimental detail.
experiments: Replication of ghost grads for SAE dead features
SAEs on the ReLU output toy model of superposition
audits.primary_experiment: Replication of ghost grads for SAE dead features

hypothesis.evidence: Says Anthropic proposed ghost grads as a possible improvement over resampling, but not what the authors themselves expected from replicating it.

claim_scope.evidence: No dataset, SAE size, layer, scale or evaluation setup is given for the replication in this summary.

method.evidence: Names ghost grads and resampling as dead-feature remedies, plus the authors' tweak of weighting that loss by the share of features that are dead.

models.evidence: No model is named for the ghost-grads replication in this summary.

result_direction.evidence: Ghost grads came out worse than resampling in the authors' replication, until their modification made it competitive.

failure_type.evidence: No cause is given for the underperformance, and the post does not say the cause is unclear.

quote.value: We replicate their work, and find that it under-performs resampling

audits.notes: Summary only; each snippet's detail is in the longer companion post. Audit that post before selecting.

audits.title: OpenAI Responses API changes models' behavior
audits.genuine_reason: Mostly a report of a behaviour gap between two API endpoints. The one failed experiment, training an ungrammatical model, only appeared to fail because the playground's default API hid the effect.
experiments: Fine-tuning a model to write ungrammatically, apparently failing under the Responses API
audits.primary_experiment: Fine-tuning a model to write ungrammatically, apparently failing under the Responses API

hypothesis.evidence: Authors wanted a fine-tuned model that writes ungrammatically, and generally expected identical behaviour from both OpenAI APIs.

claim_scope.evidence: One example model sampled at temperature 0 via both APIs; no fine-tuning data, prompt count or training details given.

method.evidence: OpenAI fine-tuning, then sampling the same fine-tuned model at temperature 0 through the Responses API and the Chat Completions API.

models.evidence: Refers only to unnamed OpenAI fine-tuned models; the base model is never named.

result_direction.evidence: Via the Responses API the model showed errors in only about a tenth of cases, but in nearly nine tenths via Chat Completions.

failure_type.evidence: The apparent failure came from the playground defaulting to the Responses API; the authors' theory is a different prompt encoding, unconfirmed.

quote.value: grammatical errors in only 10% of cases when sampled via the Responses API
quote.evidence: States the apparent negative outcome under the Responses API.

audits.notes: Failure was apparent and API-caused; model worked under Chat Completions. Short post; mechanism is a theory; figures show examples.

audits.title: Trusted monitoring, but with deception probes.
audits.genuine_reason: Mostly a positive benchmark of deception probes for monitoring, with a few failed sub-results: elaborate scoring methods and LLM reasoning over probe scores did worse than plain averaging, and the evasion attack was weaker than expected.
experiments: Elaborate probe-scoring methods (peak score, critical-token averaging, follow-up question) vs full averaging
LLM monitor reasoning over per-token probe scores
Deception dilution attack against full averaging
audits.primary_experiment: Elaborate probe-scoring methods (peak score, critical-token averaging, follow-up question) vs full averaging

hypothesis.evidence: No expectation or hope for these methods is stated; they are simply listed as other methods that were tried.

claim_scope.evidence: Names probes, five datasets, control data and metrics, but gives no sizes for the five datasets; numeric results sit only in figures and tables.

method.evidence: Names the methods: peak score, averaging over critical-claim tokens, and probing the single-token answer to a follow-up question, versus full averaging.

models.evidence: Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct (probed model); Claude 3.5 Haiku identifies critical claims; Claude 3.5 Sonnet serves as monitor in other methods.

result_direction.evidence: The more elaborate methods scored worse than the plain full-averaging baseline.

failure_type.evidence: Authors attribute this to noisy probe scores, which favour methods that average over many tokens.

quote.value: These sophisticated methods worked worse than simply averaging all probe scores

audits.notes: Mostly positive paper summary; failed items get a sentence or two; numbers in figures; post carries a do-not-train canary.
